segments.voice: Yesterday was the last day of year 3: the ranges, and the Gita's promise that no effort on this path is lost. What small step did you take? Today year four begins, with the goddess. Day one thousand sixty-two.

A king rides into a forest alone. He has lost his kingdom. Enemies beat him in battle, and then his own ministers turned on him and took the treasury. He tells himself he's out hunting. In the forest he finds a quiet hermitage, the home of a sage named Medhas, and he stays. And there, under the trees, he can't stop worrying. Is my elephant being fed? Are my servants treated well? Is the treasure I gathered being wasted? Then he meets a second man, a merchant named Samadhi, sitting there just as lost. That's how the Devi Mahatmya begins. Year four reads it whole, from its first page to its last.
screen: `A KING RIDES INTO A FOREST ALONE.` → `HE CAN'T STOP WORRYING.` → `A MERCHANT, JUST AS LOST.`

segments.voice: Devi Mahatmya means the glory of the goddess. Tradition places it inside a larger book, the Markandeya Purana, and it's also known as the Chandi. In some homes and temples it's recited from beginning to end. But notice what it opens with. Not a goddess. Two men with a problem they can't solve. The merchant's story is harder than the king's. His own wife and sons, greedy for his money, threw him out of the house. And still, he tells the king, he can't stop wondering whether they're well. Are they happy? Are they in trouble? Why does his mind keep going back to people who sent him away? So the two of them go to the sage together with one honest question. In paraphrase: we both know these things have left us. We know it. So why do we still grieve? Why doesn't knowing help? Medhas doesn't call them foolish. He points at birds: hungry themselves, they still drop grain into the beaks of their young. Every creature, he says, is pulled this way. Then he gives the pull a name. Mahamaya, the great illusion, and in this text she is the goddess herself. She seizes the minds of even the wise and drags them into confusion. And the same goddess, when she is gracious, is the one who sets people free. That's the surprise of the opening. The goddess isn't introduced first as a warrior. She's introduced as the power at work inside the very worry the king and the merchant carried into the forest. The king asks the obvious next question: who is this goddess? And Medhas begins to tell stories. The rest of the book is those stories.
screen: `TWO MEN WITH A PROBLEM.` · `WHY DOESN'T KNOWING HELP?` · `BIRDS FEEDING THEIR YOUNG.` · `MAHAMAYA BINDS, AND SETS FREE.` · then, large: `WHO IS THIS GODDESS?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one thing your mind keeps going back to. Settle, and let the breath slow. Let it come up on its own: a person, a place, a job, something that's gone and still pulls. Don't argue with it, and don't try to fix it. Just notice the pull, the way the merchant noticed his. Where do you feel it in the body? Each time you breathe out, let the grip loosen a little, without throwing away the care underneath it. If you pray, you can hold it before God or the goddess in the words you already use. If you don't, let the breath do the holding. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. The glory of the goddess: a book that begins in a forest, with two men who can't stop worrying, and a sage who names the pull.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, when your mind goes back to something that's gone, notice the pull once, kindly, and keep walking. Day one thousand sixty-two. Year four, begun.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Devi Mahatmya, also called the Chandi or Durga Saptashati, from beginning to end, especially during Navaratri, and it is recited in some temples devoted to the goddess.

original.note: Sanskrit: devī-māhātmya, the glory (greatness) of the goddess.
